item.title: Is Falling in Love Quickly a Red Flag?
item.description:
Mating

Is Falling in Love Quickly a Red Flag?

Why fast romances sometimes thrive—and sometimes explode.

Posted June 27, 2026

Key points
  • Fast-start relationships can thrive if attraction is matched by genuine admiration.
  • An emophiliac falls in love quickly and often, but doesn't always lack commitment.
  • Rapid love isn’t risky unless it leads one to overlook key aspects of their partner.
Source: Jonathan Borba / Pexels

“I love you. I knew it the minute I met you.”—Pat, Silver Linings Playbook

Falling in love is exhilarating. The real danger is not speed, but illusion. When love arrives quickly, the risk is not the intensity of attraction but the possibility that our early evaluations of a partner are incomplete or distorted.

Attractiveness and Praiseworthiness

“I didn’t fall for you. I walked into love with you, with my eyes wide open.”—Tessa Bailey

Two core evaluations underlie romantic love: attractiveness and praiseworthiness. Attractiveness—often including sexual desire—is an immediate magnet that draws people together. Praiseworthiness involves deeper assessments of a partner’s character, values, and achievements, and is closely related to profound friendship. Romantic love typically requires both: the spark of attraction and the admiration that sustains a long-term bond.

The two evaluations differ in how they emerge. Attractiveness can ignite almost instantly, whereas praiseworthiness is usually revealed gradually. Accordingly, attractiveness often fuels the intensity of early romance, while praiseworthy qualities support enduring romantic depth (Ben-Ze’ev, 2000).

Yet when either dimension is exceptionally strong, judgment can become biased. This imbalance often produces halo effects. The attractiveness halo occurs when physical beauty inflates perceptions of intelligence, morality, or sociability. The personality halo works in the opposite direction: Highly valued traits such as kindness, humor, wisdom, competence, or status enhance perceived attractiveness. Thus, people who confer social status—such as the wealthy or powerful—often appear more sexually desirable as well (Ben-Ze’ev, 2019).

Is Falling in Love Quickly a Red Flag?

“I heard about a woman who said: ‘I know this man is going to be my husband,’ and so she had sex with him on the first date and in the end, married him.”—Anonymous

Intense early attraction or admiration is not inherently problematic. Indeed, research on love at first sight suggests that idealizing a partner in the early stages can enhance later relationship quality and stability. The “honeymoon ceiling effect” similarly indicates that marital satisfaction rarely exceeds its initial peak (Proulx et al., 2017; Lorber et al., 2015). A poll of 2,000 Britons found that 59 percent of relationships that began with love at first sight were still thriving, while 19 percent had lasted more than 40 years. High-starting relationships often remain highly satisfying. The initial spark can become a durable foundation.

Rapid love becomes risky when it bypasses the slower process of discovering who the other person really is. Accordingly, the crucial question is not, “Did you fall fast?” but rather, “Did you overlook important aspects of your partner?”

When Red Flags Become More Likely

“When I love, I do it without counting. I give myself entirely. And each time, it is the grand love of my life.”—Brigitte Bardot

“Can’t stop staring at your face; I should have kissed you longer.”—Taylor Swift

Emophilia—sometimes called emotional promiscuity—is the tendency to fall in love quickly and frequently. Daniel Jones argues that emophilia is a stable personality trait in which people vary considerably. It does not make love less genuine, but it does shape how relationships begin and develop. Jones suggests that emophilia reflects an unusually active “I want you” system of romantic attraction. This differs from the “I need you” urgency characteristic of anxious attachment. He further argues that emophilia is not primarily the result of trauma or psychological dysfunction, but rather a normal individual difference that people possess to varying degrees (Jones, 2026).

Romantic needs are essential for a flourishing relationship: respect, trust, honesty, safety, kindness, and mutual growth. Romantic wants—shared interests, excitement, pleasure, and social compatibility—enhance a relationship but cannot sustain it on their own. Falling in love quickly is not itself a red flag. It becomes one when the pursuit of exciting wants distracts from the assessment of essential needs.

Although emophiliacs enjoy falling in love quickly and intensely, they do not necessarily reject long-term commitment. Some believe they simply have not yet found the right partner; others question strict romantic exclusivity. Nevertheless, their emotional openness has a potential downside. Because they can develop strong feelings for new people with relative ease, they may be more vulnerable to infidelity even while genuinely loving their current partner.

Concluding Thoughts

“Falling in love was the easy part; planning a wedding—yikes!”—Niecy Nash

Overanalyzing the early stages of romance can drain them of joy. When you first fall in love, it is natural—and often healthy—to surrender to some of the excitement. Yet once the initial emotional surge subsides, it becomes important to examine whether attraction is supported by genuine praiseworthiness.

The central difficulty for emophiliacs is not that they fall in love too quickly, but that they may fall in love too often. Frequent transitions from one intense romance to another can make it difficult to develop the profundity that characterizes enduring love. Red flags emerge not because love arrives quickly, but because excitement can sometimes replace understanding. Healthy love may begin in an instant, but it deepens through time. Speed matters less than whether attraction and admiration continue to grow as partners come to know one another more fully.

So, is falling in love quickly a red flag? Sometimes—but only when speed becomes a substitute for clarity. When it does not, a swift beginning can mark the start of a vibrant and lasting romantic bond.

item.title: The Link Between Heat and Violence
item.description:
Law and Crime

The Link Between Heat and Violence

High temperatures lower impulse control, increasing violence and crime.

Posted June 27, 2026

Key points
  • Higher temperatures increase violent, impulsive crime more than planned property crime.
  • Heat impairs judgment and allows violent impulses to take over.
  • Alcohol consumption rises with temperature, compounding the loss of impulse control.

As the planet warms, heat waves and high-temperature days are becoming more common. This is dangerous for your health. As we saw in a previous post, heat might also cloud your brain and result in poor decisions.

It might also get you killed or injured because of poor decisions by others.

In research reported by the World Bank Group, Behrer and Bolotnyy (2024) examined administrative criminal records from Texas alongside weather data and found that arrests increase by up to 15 percent on hot days. The effect was driven by increases in violent crime. That is, burglars do not choose hot days more often than cold ones for break-ins, and pickpockets do not go out more when it is hot. Rather, people more often resort to unplanned, impulsive violence when temperatures are high. As Behrer and Bolotnyy found, higher incomes and newer housing counteract these effects, likely because both factors are associated with access to air conditioning and better cooling strategies.

In another study, Blakeslee and coauthors (2021) used data from 600 police stations in India between 2011 and 2016, combined with daily weather records, to examine the relationship between crime and temperature. They found that violent, impulsive crimes, including violence against women and ethnically motivated violence, responded to both daily and seasonal temperature variation. There is more violent crime on hotter days, but also more violent crime when it is hotter at any given point during the day. Property crimes such as break-ins showed seasonal variation, but no relationship to within-day temperatures.

In the Heat of the Moment

Many other studies have reached similar conclusions. Heat increases non-property, impulsive crime more than property crime, and it has a much larger impact on violent crimes and crimes of passion.

This is not surprising. As discussed in the previous post, when temperatures are too high, your body attempts to cool you down, which, at the risk of oversimplifying a complex topic, may disrupt blood flow to the brain and result in poor judgment. When decision-making is impaired, intuition and impulses tend to take over.

If things do not go your way, it is perfectly normal to feel frustrated or even angry. Being a functioning member of society does not require suppressing all emotional reactions. It requires controlling them and not overreacting. When impulses take over, more people overreact and become physical after even minor slights, real, perceived, or imagined.

Going Outside

The simplest explanation for the correlation between high temperatures and violent crime is that heat impairs impulse control and thus increases spur-of-the-moment aggression. But the picture is more complicated.

Cohen and Gonzalez (2024) combined administrative records, surveys on unreported crime, and daily weather reports to study the relationship between temperature and crime in Mexico. They found that for every 1°C increase in temperature, criminal charges increase by 1.78 percent, even at comfortable temperatures. As in many other studies, the effects are stronger for violent crimes, including homicides, sexual crimes, and family violence.

Cohen and Gonzalez also found that part of the increase in violent crime on hot days is related to changes in how people spend their time. When it is hot, people spend more time outside their homes. Since the large majority of violent crimes occur outside the victim's home, part of the increase is simply a matter of exposure and opportunity. For example, the temperature's effect on crime is much stronger on weekends than on weekdays, when people have more freedom as to where they spend their time.

There is one more factor. When it is hot, people drink more fluids, as they should. But they also drink more alcohol, which lowers impulse control further. In Cohen and Gonzalez's data, around 29 percent of all weather-induced crimes were committed by drunk offenders.

Beware of Hot Days

As discussed in the previous post, heat might cloud your judgment. It might also cloud the judgment of those around you. Even if you remain calm and controlled, on a hot day, you might be more likely to be drawn into a situation that would be better avoided.

First, be alert to other people's tempers. Nobody is fully rational, and heat does not help. Give people space, defuse rather than escalate, and stay cool.

Second, think carefully about where you place yourself. A hot day may not be the best occasion to explore an unfamiliar neighbourhood or one where alcohol is flowing freely. When in doubt, stick to public places with visible security (and AC).

Third, check yourself. If you can have a short temper on occasion, make an extra effort on hot days. Cool down, drink water, stay in the shade. Your fellow human beings, and probably the people closest to you, will be grateful.

item.title: All Dogs Are Saying, Is Give Pees a Chance
item.description:
Animal Behavior

All Dogs Are Saying, Is Give Pees a Chance

Research shows dogs pee for a variety of reasons, but detailed data are lacking.

Posted June 27, 2026

Key points
  • There are many reasons why dogs pee when, where, and how they do, and peeing is not always scent-marking.
  • Different patterns of peeing are a testament to the amazing social, cognitive, and emotional lives of dogs.
  • Possible messages of peeing and scent-marking could be related to gender, mood, status, or territory.
  • Giving pees the chance to be decoded from the dogs' point of view will benefit our relationships with them.
Source: Jonas Thulin/Used with permission

One of the most frequent questions I'm asked about dog behavior deals with peeing. I usually say something simple like, "Dogs pee for a wide variety of reasons, and there's lots to learn."

This typically results in my asking why the person is asking me these questions, and then we often have a nice conversation that opens the door to many wonderful chats about the basic question: "Why do dogs pee when, where, and how they do?"

This is why I decided to write this brief guide to dogs' peeing patterns and what they might mean. Most, if not all, dogs would benefit from their own and others' humans giving pees a chance to explain themselves so that their canine ways of urinating are better understood and appreciated. Here, I'm playing off a wonderful phrase from dog trainer Jonas Thulin, who always exclaims, "Give pees a chance."

Let's see what science, stories, and some common sense tell us about patterns of canine peeing. Much of what I write here can be found in Dogs Demystified: An A-to-Z Guide to All Things Canine and has been updated to include more recent data.

Different ways of peeing and sending pee-mail

Simple peeing occurs when dogs urinate simply to empty their bladder because they have to go.

Scent-marking occurs when a dog intentionally pees in a specific place to convey information to other dogs, another form of sending “pee-mail.” Marking is different from merely randomly peeing anywhere when a dog simply has to go and it doesn’t matter where they do it. Messages from scent-marking could be related to gender, mood, status, or territory, something along the lines of, "This is my space, stay out." More research is definitely needed to get a solid handle on scent-marking.1 Frankly, I think most dogs wish they could pee on everything in the world, and some do just that.

Dry-marking occurs when a dog, usually a male, lifts a leg without peeing. I studied dry-marking extensively and wondered if the dry-marking dog might be trying to send a visual signal, such as "I’m peeing—this is my territory." They also might be trying to get another dog to use up all their pee by over-marking. On occasion, male dogs will lift a leg and not urinate—perhaps they’re faking it—and then they walk a few feet and immediately lift a leg and pee. Similar behavior has been observed among free-ranging dogs living outside of Rome by Simona Cafazzo and her colleagues.

Over-marking occurs when a dog pees or occasionally poops over the pee or poop of another dog. This form of pee-mail might be used when a dog is trying to mask another dog's odor to say something like, "This is my territory, not yours."

"Pissing matches" is a colloquial term for repeated over-marking between two or more dogs and occurs when one dog pees over another dog’s urine and the other dog immediately returns the favor. I’ve seen hundreds, if not thousands, of pissing matches during the enormous amount of time I’ve spent at dog parks and watching dogs pass one another on leash. Sometimes they make me and others break out laughing at this seemingly endless game.

While most pissing matches take place outdoors, this is not always the case. A few years ago, my cycling teammate John Talley and his wife, Tyla, told me about an ongoing pissing match between their two dogs, Rigby and Bodie. Bodie was Rigby’s father, but Rigby joined the Talley household first. Once Rigby was nicely settled in and house-trained, Bodie arrived already house-trained, but once Bodie started peeing inside for whatever reason, Rigby did, too. It also turned out that Rigby always had to have the last pee. In addition, Bodie would ground scratch after peeing, and this had become part of their ongoing pissing contests. Tyla told me that Rigby never had ground scratched before Bodie came along, and Rigby began doing it even if Bodie wasn't around. Is this a territorial battle? Is Bodie just doing what dogs do in a new habitat, and is Rigby, into whose home Bodie intruded, just “defending” his place? I honestly don’t know. As far as I can determine, these sorts of indoor pissing matches are very rare, but they might be a way of working out problems associated with living in a shared space without fighting that could result in serious injuries or death.

Size matters: Research shows that some small male dogs apparently try to exaggerate their size when peeing or marking, and that small male dogs urinate more than large male dogs, perhaps indicating a preference for peeing or scent-marking over direct interactions that could be risky. The researchers had hypothesized that small male dogs would benefit more than large male dogs from exaggerating their size, and they found that small dogs raised their legs higher (or at a higher angle) in proportion to their size than large males to leave higher urine marks.

It's interesting to ponder if the small dogs were trying to be dishonest by exaggerating their size, and does this mean small dogs have a “little dog complex”? I had never previously thought that small dogs might intentionally try to make themselves “look” bigger by trying to deposit pee at higher heights and found this to be a fascinating discovery in need of more research.

Coda: It's essential to become fluent in "Dog"

Many of the proposed functions of simply peeing and marking aren't mutually exclusive, and all should be explored through detailed research. Most research on peeing has been conducted on laboratory or homed dogs, and more data are needed for free-ranging individuals who can move here and there when they want to.

There is still much to learn about peeing and pee-mail. And, given the complexity of this behavior and the many messages that might be transmitted by the scent itself—how it is deposited, where it is sprayed, and the many reasons why a dog is doing what they are doing—simple answers aren't to be expected. This is a tribute to the amazing social, cognitive, and emotional lives of the dogs themselves, who can alter their behavior to do what's needed when they encounter pee.

The need for more data is why dogs might be saying you need to know more about their peeing patterns, to give pees a chance to be decoded from our point of view, and give them a chance to do what we want them to do before offering misleading human-centric explanations. You must become fluent in "Dog."

All in all, when we learn more about why dogs pee from their point of view, it will be good for us and for them—a win-win for all.

item.title: A 21st-Century Luddite Critique of Digital Work
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

A 21st-Century Luddite Critique of Digital Work

Luddite resistance anticipated today’s psychological fallout from digitization.

Posted June 27, 2026

Key points
  • The Luddite critique of technology's harm to identity, agency, and social belonging is still relevant today.
  • Digital platforms intensify polarization and erode trust, threatening societal mental stability.
  • Tech benefits are unevenly distributed, fostering inequality, alienation, and social comparison.

The Luddites are often portrayed as irrational, reactionary machine-breakers, but psychological consideration reveals something far more nuanced and relevant for the digital age.

Luddite resistance to the increasingly widespread introduction of industrial machinery in the early 19th century stemmed from their awareness of how technological change disrupts wellbeing—particularly in terms of human identity, agency, and social belonging1. Reconsidered in the context of digital technology and artificial intelligence (AI), the Luddite critique appears less like hostility to progress, and more like an early warning about the psychological costs of poorly governed innovation.

Core Questions Raised by the Luddite Movement

At its core, the Luddite movement poses a question that resonates within contemporary psychology: What happens to the human mind in systems designed primarily for efficiency, rather than well-being?

The original Luddites did not object to technology, but rather to its "fraudulent" introduction that degraded skilled labour and reduced workers to repetitive, fragmented functionaries.1 Such changes undermine intrinsic motivation and autonomy, which are key components of well-being, as identified in self-determination theory.2 When individuals lose control over their work and are treated as interchangeable, expendable "cogs in a machine," their sense of purpose and self-worth is eroded.3 This underlies part of the Marxist critique of capital, but can just as easily be understood from a humanitarian or even a profit-driven perspective (if your workers are unhappy, productivity takes a nosedive4—all but the most incompetent of managers know this).

Luddite Concerns in the Digital and AI Era

Such well-being concerns raised by the Luddites have intensified in the digital age. AI, we are told, is increasingly capable of performing cognitively demanding tasks (how well it performs such tasks is still under some question). Although this may bring short-term economic benefits, based on employing fewer people, it creates disturbing psychological challenges.5-8 Work is a central source of identity, structure, and meaning for many people,5 and unemployment and job insecurity are associated with poorer mental health outcomes, including anxiety and depression.6 The displacement or de-skilling of workers by AI, therefore, represents both an economic shift and a psychological attack—potentially leading to widespread loss of purpose and social disintegration.7

The replacement of people by AI exemplifies such Luddite-recognised tensions in their clearest form. From a financial perspective, automation may temporarily enhance productivity and reduce costs. Yet, it risks eroding key sources of meaning, stability, and identity. Even if a society does become more efficient, individuals may experience increased anxiety, alienation, and purposelessness. This bifurcation of economic and psychological outcomes lies at the heart of the Luddite critique, and ultimately undermines the very financial benefits that drove their adoption.

Even when jobs are not eliminated by AI, the transformation of the nature of the work carries psychological costs. The use of generative AI reduces demand for labour in some roles, and increases performance pressures and skill requirements in others. This creates an environment of uncertainty as well as new demands and cognitive overload, where workers are made to continuously adapt to remain relevant and employed.8 Such conditions are likely to lead to burnout and reduce overall well-being, particularly among individuals with fewer resources or lower digital literacy.8

Impact of Unequal Distribution of Technological Benefits

The unequal distribution of technological benefits across society further compounds these effects. Evidence suggests that workers with strong digital skills may be able to hold on longer against the cheaper AI, while others face marginalisation9—both economic and social. This uneven situation contributes to feelings of relative deprivation and fosters social comparison—both processes known to harm mental health and increase dissatisfaction. The result is not merely economic inequality, but a widening gap in perceived competence, status, and life satisfaction—outcomes central to healthy psychological functioning.10

Effects of Digital Technology Beyond the Workplace

Beyond the workplace, it is well known that digital technologies affect cognition, emotion, and social relationships. Overuse of social media platforms has long been associated with mental health concerns, particularly among adolescents.11 Longitudinal evidence suggests that heavy use is linked to a higher risk of depression and poorer well-being. These effects can be understood through mechanisms such as social comparison, reduced sleep quality, and incentive-motivation system dysregulation from exposure to constant feedback loops (likes, shares, notifications).11

Moreover, digital platforms reshape how individuals process information and relate to others. Algorithms that prioritise engagement tend to amplify emotionally charged and polarising content, reinforcing cognitive biases and in-group identities.12,13 Increased political polarisation is associated with greater susceptibility to misinformation and reduced willingness to engage with out-group members.12 At a societal level, misinformation has been identified as a major threat to trust and cohesion, eroding the shared realities that underpin collective mental stability.14 These dynamics highlight how digital environments can distort, not only individual cognition, but also the psychological foundations of social life—a key component of the Luddite critique.

The Luddite Call for Human-Centred Innovation

What unites these various harms is that they are not incidental, nor accidental, consequences of the uptake of digital technology; they are inescapably inherent in the very design of digital systems. Technologies optimised for efficiency, profit, or the generation of sustained attention neglect psychological needs, such as autonomy, competence, and relatedness. This reflects a broader pattern that the Luddites recognised: Technology is never neutral. It embodies particular values that tend to prioritise economic gains for certain individuals over human flourishing. Two hundred years ago, the Luddites resisted forms of technological deployment that harmed workers and communities.1 If truth be told, it was the 1809 repeal of Edward VI’s 1552 law banning gig mills—a form of technology seen as destructive to the economics and well-being of "croppers" (wool workers)—that sparked much Luddite protest. Thus, the Luddite position, along with some of Edward VI’s industrial policies, is actually an example of "human-centred design" or "well-being-oriented policy."

Contemporary Relevance of the Luddite Critique

In this light, the Luddites can be understood, not as opponents of progress, but as early theorists of its psychological consequences, and providers of a subtle socio-economic platform (distantly echoed in B.F. Skinner’s Walden Two, showing an often ignored subtlety in Skinner’s work). Their insistence on questioning who benefits from technology, and at what human cost, remains profoundly relevant. As digital technologies continue to reshape work, relationships, and cognition, Luddite warnings serve as a reminder that progress should be measured by its capacity to sustain and enhance human well-being, not by the economic power that it brings to its purveyors.
